macro.label: Unit architecture
macro.tip: Structures a whole sequence of 4–15 lessons

meso.label: Multi-lesson routine
meso.tip: An investigation or routine across a few lessons, nestable in a unit

micro.label: Single lesson
micro.tip: A strategy for one lesson or activity

dial.label: Guidance dial
dial.tip: Calibrates teacher guidance within any model

DIMS.label: What is the main learning purpose?
DIMS.sub: Choose one, or two if the sequence genuinely has a dual purpose.
DIMS.help: Purpose drives the choice more than anything else. A misconception-focused sequence needs cognitive conflict; an argument-focused one needs structured critique; a design-focused one needs a problem with real constraints.
options: Explain a phenomenon with a model
Solve a real problem or design

DIMS.label: How much time do you have?
DIMS.help: Models that hand students control (problem-based, project-based, Ambitious Science Teaching) need time for false starts and revision. Short timeframes favour tighter sequences.
options: A depth study or term project

DIMS.label: How independent are your learners with inquiry?
DIMS.help: Novices lack the knowledge to manage open-ended tasks, so low-guidance models overload them (Kirschner, Sweller & Clark, 2006). Readiness is about experience with inquiry, not ability.

DIMS.label: What kind of concept is it?
DIMS.help: Observable phenomena suit hands-on exploration. Abstract, unobservable mechanisms (particles, genes, fields) need explicit modelling. Large-scale or historical ideas rely on data and models. Value-laden topics need ethical reasoning.

DIMS.label: How well known are students’ alternative conceptions?
DIMS.help: Robust, well-documented ideas (for example, a moving object needs a force to keep moving) call for models built around eliciting and challenging them.

DIMS.label: Which Working scientifically outcomes are you targeting?
DIMS.sub: Select all that apply (Stage 4 SC4-WS or Stage 5 SC5-WS).
DIMS.help: Different models build different skills. Inquiry models build planning and conducting; argument models build analysing and communicating; problem and design models build problem-solving.

DIMS.label: How confident are you facilitating open-ended discussion and inquiry?
DIMS.help: Some models ask the teacher to withhold answers, manage disagreement and follow students’ ideas. That is a learnable skill; choose a model that stretches you without derailing the class.

DIMS.label: What practical resources do you have?
DIMS.help: Some models depend on hands-on work. Without a lab, simulations (such as PhET) and secondary data sets can carry the Explore phase.

DIMS.label: What evidence of learning do you need?
DIMS.help: Align the model with the assessment. A design product suits a design cycle; a written argument suits ADI or SWH; a conceptual explanation suits 5E, GLM or Ambitious Science Teaching.

DIMS.label: How high are the language demands for your class?
DIMS.help: Classes with many EAL/D learners benefit from shared concrete experience before technical language, and from structured writing scaffolds. Talk-heavy models need extra support.

DIMS.label: Is there scope for place-based learning with local community?
DIMS.help: Some models make authentic space for local contexts and Aboriginal knowledges. Develop these with local Aboriginal community and your school’s Aboriginal Education staff.
